content: The group of phages identified as Bacteroides fragilis HSP40 phages is unique because they are exclusively found in human feces and are absent in animal feces. These phages are present in relatively low numbers in sewage and are nearly undetectable in certain geographical regions. B. fragilis HSP40 phages belong to the Siphoviridae family, characterized by flexible, non-contractile tails, double-stranded DNA, and capsids with diameters of up to 60 nm. Another group of Bacteroides phages, which use B. fragilis strain RYC2056 as a host, exhibits a broader spectrum of occurrence. These phages are found in the feces of both humans and various animals. Their numbers in sewage are significantly higher than those of B. fragilis HSP40 phages. Bacteroides bacteriophages have been proposed as potential indicators of fecal pollution due to their specific association with fecal material and their exceptional resistance to environmental conditions. Notably, B. fragilis HSP40 phages are exclusively associated with human feces. A representative member of the B. fragilis HSP40 phages, Bacteroides fragilis phage B40-8, has demonstrated greater resistance to inactivation by chlorine compared to poliovirus type 1, simian rotavirus SA11, coliphage f2, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus faecalis. Similarly, phages using B. fragilis strain RYC2056 as a host also exhibit relative resistance to disinfection. However, a limitation of B. fragilis phages, particularly HSP40 phages, is their relatively low abundance in sewage and polluted water environments. Human enteric viruses have been detected in drinking water supplies that tested negative for B. fragilis HSP40 phages, highlighting the limitations of these phages as indicators. B. fragilis HSP40 phages are excreted by approximately 10–20% of humans in certain regions, resulting in their substantially lower numbers in sewage compared to somatic and F-RNA coliphages. For instance, a mean count of 67 B. fragilis HSP40 phages per liter has been reported in a sewage-polluted river. In some parts of the world, these phages are undetectable in sewage. In contrast, phages using B. fragilis RYC2056 as a host are excreted in larger numbers and are more universally distributed, with over 25% of humans excreting them on average. In water environments, B. fragilis HSP40 phages have been found to outnumber cytopathogenic enteric viruses by only about fivefold on average. Theoretically, higher levels of B. fragilis phages would be expected in wastewater than those detected. This discrepancy may be attributed to insufficiently anaerobic conditions during plaque assays. Improved detection methods could lead to higher recorded numbers of B. fragilis phages in sewage and polluted water environments. The practical application of B. fragilis phages is limited by the complexity and cost of detection methods compared to coliphages. These methods require the use of antibiotics for selection and the incubation of cultures and plaque assays under strict anaerobic conditions. Results from plaque assays typically take about 24 hours, compared to approximately 8 hours for coliphages. The presence of B. fragilis phages in drinking water is strong evidence of fecal pollution and shortcomings in water treatment and disinfection processes. Specifically, the detection of B. fragilis HSP40 phages indicates fecal pollution of human origin. However, their low numbers in sewage, polluted water, and drinking water supplies imply that the absence of B. fragilis phages in treated drinking water does not confirm the absence of pathogens such as enteric viruses and protozoan parasites. Enteric viruses, which infect the human gastrointestinal tract and are predominantly transmitted via the fecal-oral route, include well-known members such as enteroviruses, astroviruses, adenoviruses, orthoreoviruses, rotaviruses, caliciviruses, and hepatitis A and E viruses. These viruses are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. They differ in structure, composition, nucleic acid type, morphology, excretion rates, environmental survival, and resistance to water treatment processes. Enteric viruses possess robust capsids that enable them to survive harsh environmental conditions and pass through the acidic and proteolytic environment of the stomach to infect susceptible epithelial cells in the duodenum. The use of enteric viruses as indicator organisms is based on the limitations of existing indicators. Fecal bacteria differ significantly from enteric viruses in terms of survival in water environments and sensitivity to treatment and disinfection processes. Monitoring based on representative enteric viruses would provide more valuable information about the presence of these viruses in water and their response to control measures. Enteric viruses are excreted by individuals worldwide at rates and in numbers that result in their universal presence in substantial quantities in wastewater. However, the prevalence of individual viruses may vary due to differences in infection and excretion rates. During outbreaks, much higher numbers of enteric viruses would be present. Practical methods for routine monitoring of water supplies for a broad spectrum of enteric viruses are not yet available. Viruses such as enteroviruses, adenoviruses, and orthoreoviruses are more readily detectable and occur in relatively high numbers in polluted environments. These viruses can be detected using practical and moderately cost-effective techniques based on cytopathogenic effects in cell culture, yielding results within 3–12 days depending on the virus type. Advances in technology and expertise are reducing costs, making testing for cytopathogenic viruses in drinking water supplies more feasible for certain purposes. Testing could validate the effectiveness of treatment processes and verify process performance in specific investigations. However, the incubation times, costs, and relative complexity of testing make enteric virus testing unsuitable for operational or verification monitoring. The presence of any enteric viruses in drinking water should be regarded as an indicator of potential contamination by other enteric viruses, conclusive evidence of fecal pollution, and evidence of shortcomings in water treatment and disinfection processes.
